transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in today because... well, I've barely been sleeping lately. It started after a warehouse inspection I had to do for work. I just lie in bed at night, and I keep replaying bits of what happened over and over in my head. And even when I finally do manage to drift off, I wake up completely drenched in sweat, wide awake, and my heart is racing like I'm right back near that blast. It's just... it's exhausting, and I need some help.
During that warehouse inspection, did something happen that was life-threatening or that made you feel like your life was in serious danger?

Yeah, um... like I mentioned, there was a blast. I was just doing a standard walkthrough of the building, and then out of nowhere, this explosion happened. I don't really know the specifics of what went wrong or how close I actually was to the worst of it, but... yeah, in that moment, I absolutely thought I was going to die. It definitely felt like my life was in serious danger.

When did these symptoms—the replaying of what happened, the nightmares, the sweating, and the racing heart—first start after the blast? Did they begin right away that same day, or did they start a few days later?
They started pretty much right away. It's been going on for about a week now, basically ever since the day of the inspection when the explosion happened.

Besides the sleep problems and nightmares, has this experience affected your ability to work, spend time with family, or do other things you normally do? Are you having trouble functioning in your daily life?

Yeah, it really has, mostly at work. I'm an insurance underwriter, and... well, I've actually missed deadlines on several underwriting reviews this past week. I've also started handing off these industrial account calls that I'm supposed to manage myself. I just... I can't really deal with them right now. It's making me look pretty unreliable in a role I just recently took on.
Have you been trying to avoid things that remind you of the blast—like avoiding certain places, not wanting to talk about it, or staying away from work-related tasks?

Yeah, I have. Um... like I mentioned with handing off the work, I've just been letting any calls about industrial accounts go straight to voicemail. And I've been completely avoiding the specific file for that warehouse. I just... I can't look at it. Honestly, even just opening those emails makes my stomach drop, so I'm just staying away from it all as much as I can.
You mentioned these symptoms started about a week ago. Are they staying about the same intensity, or have they been getting better, worse, or changing over that week?

Um... I haven't really noticed much of a change, honestly. It feels like it's been pretty much the exact same intensity the whole time. I wouldn't say it's getting worse, but it's definitely not getting any better yet. It's just been... a constant thing all week.

You mentioned the symptoms started right after the blast about a week ago. Just to be clear—have these symptoms been happening continuously every single day since the blast, or have there been days when you felt better and the symptoms weren't as intense or weren't there at all?

Yeah, it's been every single day. There haven't really been any days where I felt better or got a break from it. It's just... this has been going on continuously for about a week now, basically ever since that warehouse inspection where the explosion happened.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with acute stress disorder following a life-threatening traumatic event (warehouse explosion). Key diagnostic features include: (1) exposure to a qualifying traumatic stressor with genuine threat to life, (2) onset of symptoms within hours/same day of trauma, (3) intrusive re-experiencing (intrusive memories, nightmares), (4) avoidance behaviors (avoiding warehouse file, industrial account calls, voicemail avoidance), (5) hyperarousal symptoms (nighttime sweating, racing heart, sleep disturbance), (6) functional impairment (missed work deadlines, unable to manage assigned tasks), and (7) continuous symptom presence for one week. The acute onset (within 24 hours) and one-week duration place this clearly within the acute stress disorder timeframe (3 days to 1 month post-trauma), rather than PTSD which requires symptom duration of at least one month.
